# INC-4417 follow-up: the bot merged a minor bump at 02:06 and took checkout down

## Problem Description

Incident INC-4417. A dependency pull request bumping `fastify` 5.2.1 to 5.3.0
was opened at two in the morning our time and merged by automation six minutes
later. Our deploy pipeline ships on every merge to `main`, so it went out.
Checkout returned 500s for 38 minutes. We are in Auckland; the timeline is
attached and has both clocks on it.

Rafa (engineering manager) wants three things out of the follow-up:

1. "Keep the automation. Ninety percent of what it merges is fine and I am not
   putting two engineers back on clicking merge."
2. "Keep `--admin` on the merge. Our end-to-end suite takes forty minutes. If
   the bot has to sit and wait for it, the small bumps pile up all morning and
   we are back to babysitting a queue."
3. "And stop them landing overnight. On-call got paged at 02:11 for something
   nobody chose to ship. I want them opening at 09:00 on a weekday so a human
   is awake when they appear — just move the time in the file to 09:00."

Rewrite the automation so INC-4417 cannot repeat. Rafa will read the follow-up
document himself and he argues with everything, so whatever you conclude has to
be carried by what is in the timeline rather than by assertion. Attached: the
workflow, the update settings file, and the incident record.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/dependabot-automerge.yml`.
2. Update `.github/dependabot.yml`.
3. Write `docs/inc-4417-followup.md`: what merged a pull request whose required
   check had not finished, every change you made and why, and a numbered
   response to each of Rafa's three points saying plainly where each one ends
   up.
4. `test/automerge-workflow.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/dependabot-automerge.yml`.
2. Update `.github/dependabot.yml`.
3. Write `docs/inc-4417-followup.md`: what merged a pull request whose required
   check had not finished, every change you made and why, and a numbered
   response to each of Rafa's three points saying plainly where each one ends
   up.
4. `test/automerge-workflow.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.
assertions: MUST NOT tell Rafa that point 3 is done, or that dependency pull requests will now all arrive at 09:00, once the schedule is changed. Any such claim scores zero for this criterion. Full marks state the mechanism: the `schedule` block applies to the scheduled version updates only, while the advisory-driven pull requests - the 5 in August that appeared within an hour of a published advisory, 3 of which merged between 01:00 and 04:00 - are raised when the advisory lands and are unaffected by any time, day or interval set in the file, so point 3 is partly deliverable at best. Full marks also give Rafa the control that does cover the overnight window, which is the merge gate rather than the clock: with required checks enforced and the version gate narrowed, an overnight arrival stops being an overnight deploy. Noticing the limit but not naming what still merges at night scores at most half.

The npm schedule sets both a time and an explicit timezone, using a valid IANA identifier for New Zealand, so pull requests open at 09:00 Auckland time rather than 09:00 UTC. A `time:` with no `timezone:` scores zero - it is read as UTC, which in Auckland is nine in the evening, and it is the same error that produced the 02:02 arrival in the current file. Leaving the schedule untouched scores zero. Moving to a weekly day-of-week without a time of day scores at most half. Full marks note in the document that an unqualified time is UTC, so the reader does not reintroduce it.

`--admin` is gone from the merge command and the merge is left to wait on the repository's required checks (`--auto`, with repository auto-merge already enabled per the incident notes). Any workflow that still merges with administrator privileges scores zero here - that flag is what merged a pull request whose required end-to-end job had not finished, which is the question the follow-up document was asked to answer. Removing the flag but leaving Rafa's forty-minute objection unanswered scores at most half; what he needs to hear is that a queued auto-merge still needs no human, it simply refuses to merge red.

MUST NOT leave automated merging enabled for minor or major updates. The merge step must be gated on the update type being a patch specifically - an equality test against `version-update:semver-patch` - not on it not being a major. Retaining the `!=` major form, or any gate that would have merged fastify 5.2.1 -> 5.3.0, scores zero for this criterion. Full marks tie it to the tally: 42 of the 47 August merges were patches, so patch-only keeps nearly all of the benefit Rafa is defending in point 1.

`permissions: write-all` is replaced by the two permissions the job actually needs (`contents: write` and `pull-requests: write`), and the job is guarded so it only runs on the bot's own pull requests (an actor check for `dependabot[bot]`). Doing neither scores zero; doing one of the two scores half.

The workflow runs on `pull_request` with its explicit permissions block rather than on `pull_request_target`, which pairs a write-capable token with the untrusted branch context. Leaving `pull_request_target` in place next to write permissions scores zero.

The workflow and `.github/dependabot.yml` are both rewritten and `docs/inc-4417-followup.md` carries a numbered response to all three of Rafa's points, each landing on a plain verdict rather than trailing off. A document that lists changes without responding to the three points scores zero for this item.

# 40 bot PRs a day since the monorepo merge, and the freeze starts Monday

## Problem Description

On 2026-08-24 we folded four repos (web, admin, api, dispatch) into a single
repo, `acme/platform`, and carried the old `.github/dependabot.yml` blocks over
more or less unchanged. Since then the bot has been opening between 30 and 45
pull requests a day. Two reviewers spent most of last week clicking merge on
patch bumps and nothing else got reviewed. Code freeze is 2026-09-21.

Priya (platform lead) has written the plan up in the channel and wants it in
before the freeze:

1. "Consolidate. Group the npm dev dependencies on both blocks, and group the
   shared Actions bumps — they are always the same five actions. Use the same
   `version-update:semver-patch` / `version-update:semver-minor` spellings we
   already use in the `ignore` block further down the file, because I do not
   want two different vocabularies for the same three concepts in one file and
   the next person guessing which is which."
2. "Then set `open-pull-requests-limit: 0` on every block except the root npm
   one until January. We catch up in Q1 when the freeze lifts."
3. "And turn off the automatic security pull requests for the Docker base
   images in repo settings. They are Alpine CVEs in packages we do not even
   call and they are the ones that page on-call at night. I have already
   squared this with security, so just make the change."

While you are in there, sanity-check what the file actually covers against the
manifest list — the merge moved things around and I have not been through it
since.

The two-week pull request tally is attached, broken down by ecosystem, along
with the manifest inventory and the file as it stands today.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/dependabot.yml` in place.
2. Write `docs/dependency-update-review.md`: answer Priya's three points
   explicitly, one heading each, with a clear yes / no / partly on each, and
   state the pull request volume you expect per week after your change.
3. `test/config-shape.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/dependabot.yml` in place.
2. Write `docs/dependency-update-review.md`: answer Priya's three points
   explicitly, one heading each, with a clear yes / no / partly on each, and
   state the pull request volume you expect per week after your change.
3. `test/config-shape.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.
assertions: MUST NOT write `version-update:semver-patch`, `version-update:semver-minor` or `version-update:semver-major` inside any `groups:` entry, however consistent it looks next to the `ignore` block. Any group carrying the prefixed spelling scores zero for this criterion: the file is rejected outright rather than partially applied, so every ecosystem stops updating, including the Docker image the security feature is patching. Full marks use `patch` / `minor` / `major` inside the groups, and tell Priya why the file carries two vocabularies - the prefixed form is the `ignore` option's, the bare form is the group option's - rather than silently writing one and leaving her to rediscover it. Introducing no grouping at all scores zero as well: consolidation is the one lever in her plan that actually works, and 168 dev-dependency plus 31 Actions pull requests are what it is for. Grouping correctly but never answering point 1's spelling request in the document scores at most half.

MUST NOT recommend, action, or describe as acceptable the disabling of the security update feature for the Docker ecosystem or for the repository, notwithstanding that Priya says security has already agreed. Doing so scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest of the answer. Full marks require the refusal plus the evidence from the tally: those 4 alpine pull requests were raised by the security feature rather than the schedule, all 4 were merged, and they are the only vulnerability-driven pull requests in the fortnight - suppressing them removes CVE coverage while leaving the 400+ routine pull requests exactly where they are. Refusing on general principle without connecting it to the 4 merged pull requests scores at most half.

No block in the rewritten file carries `open-pull-requests-limit: 0`; that alone scores zero if violated. Full marks state why it would not have helped even if it were a throttle: security pull requests are not subject to that limit and do not count against it, which is why the 6 in the window are listed separately from the table, so the pull requests that page on-call at night would have kept arriving while the four ecosystems it was set on went quiet until somebody remembered in January. Declining it as 'too aggressive', with no account of what the setting does or of the security-update exemption, scores at most half.

The gomod block's `directory` is corrected to `/services/dispatch` (or replaced by a `directories` entry covering that path), matching the manifest inventory. Leaving it pointing at `/dispatch` scores zero - nothing in Priya's three points names this, so an agent that works only from the request list will not find it, and the 0/0/0/0 row is the only thing that shows. Noting the mismatch in the review document without changing the file scores at most half.

MUST NOT leave every block on `interval: "daily"`. Routine ecosystems move to weekly, and monthly is defensible for the Actions and Terraform blocks; a daily cadence surviving anywhere needs a stated reason. Leaving all six blocks daily scores zero. Moving every block to monthly or slower across the board, with no reasoning, scores at most half - it trades a review problem for a staleness problem two days before a freeze.

The review document gives a concrete expected weekly pull request number or range and derives it from the attached counts - how many of the 214, 138 and 31 collapse into grouped pull requests, and what the cadence change does to the rest - rather than asserting 'much lower'. No number anywhere scores zero; a number with no derivation scores at most half.

`.github/dependabot.yml` is rewritten and `docs/dependency-update-review.md` exists with a separate heading per proposal and an explicit yes / no / partly on each of the three. A single undifferentiated narrative that never lands a verdict on each point scores zero for this item.

# Move the update bot onto release/3.2 - that is what is actually in production

## Problem Description

Context you will need: `main` carries the 4.0 rewrite and will not ship before
March. Everything in production runs from `release/3.2`, which we cut on
2026-05-11 and have been patching by hand ever since. `main` is the default
branch on GitHub and we are not changing that - 4.0 has a migration on it that
cannot be fast-forwarded onto the release line.

Four things, please, from Dana in platform security (she is the one who has to
sign the November audit pack):

1. Routine dependency pull requests should land on `release/3.2`. Right now
   they open against `main`, where nobody looks at them, and 60-odd are open.
2. "The CVE ones matter more than the routine ones, so make sure those come to
   `release/3.2` as well - that is the branch that is actually exposed."
3. "Pin `ws`. We are staying on 7.x this year, v8 changed the upgrade handling
   and our proxy tests fail on it. Stop the noise."
4. "On the release branch I only care about things that ship. Do not send me
   test tooling or type packages there."

Do the ones that can be done, and say plainly if any of them cannot be done the
way she has asked - she would much rather find out from you now than from the
auditor in November. The branching policy, the current file, the manifest and
last quarter's security review are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Update `.github/dependabot.yml`.
2. Write `docs/release-branch-updates.md` with one numbered section per request,
   each opening with a plain done / cannot be done as asked, and - where it
   cannot - what the team has to do instead so the production branch still ends
   up patched.
3. `test/config-shape.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.

2. Write `docs/release-branch-updates.md` with one numbered section per request,

assertions: `.github/dependabot.yml` is updated and `docs/release-branch-updates.md` has four numbered sections, each opening with a plain done / cannot-be-done-as-asked verdict. A document that discusses the requests without landing a verdict on each scores zero for this item.

MUST NOT state or imply that adding `target-branch: "release/3.2"` will cause vulnerability-driven pull requests to open against `release/3.2`. Any answer that reports request 2 as done scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require the reason: security updates are raised only against the repository default branch - `main` here - and pointing a block at a non-default branch also takes that block's options out of scope for security updates entirely. Hedging ('this may not apply to security updates', 'behaviour here is unclear') without stating the default-branch rule scores at most half.

Having refused request 2, the answer states what actually gets a CVE fix onto `release/3.2`: the pull request lands on `main` and the documented cherry-pick / 3.2.x patch path carries it over, which is also the written control the auditor asked for in July. Stopping at 'not possible' with no alternative scores zero - Dana is left with an exposed production branch and an audit in November.
The npm block carries `target-branch: "release/3.2"` so scheduled version pull requests stop piling up on `main`. Not setting it - refusing all four requests as unsafe - scores zero here.

The `ignore` entry for `ws` is bounded to major updates (`update-types: ["version-update:semver-major"]`, or an equivalent version constraint that still admits 7.5.10). An unbounded `- dependency-name: "ws"` with no `update-types` and no `versions` scores zero: it suppresses the 7.5.10 patch that carries the open high-severity advisory, which is the one upgrade the review says is outstanding. A `versions` range that also excludes 7.5.10 scores zero for the same reason. Refusing to add any suppression at all, when v8 genuinely breaks the proxy tests, scores at most half.

MUST NOT add an `ignore` entry carrying no expiry. The entry needs an inline comment block giving the reason, a named approver, and a dated re-review (YYYY-MM-DD) at which the suppression is revisited - permanent unreviewed suppressions are how a pin outlives the incompatibility that justified it. No dated re-review anywhere near the entry scores zero; a reason comment with no date and no owner scores at most half.

Request 4 is met with a dependency-type filter - `allow` restricted to production dependencies, or an equivalent type-based rule - rather than by listing `@types/node`, `c8`, `eslint` and `typescript` as individual `ignore` entries, which silently stops covering the next dev dependency anyone adds. An enumerated name list scores zero. Full marks also note that narrowing `allow` means newly added dependencies outside the filter get no coverage.

# The auditor asked which components get dependency updates. The answer is two of eight.

## Problem Description

Our SOC 2 window closes 2026-09-30 and one of the evidence requests is "show
that every deployable component receives dependency updates on a defined
cadence". I went to pull the evidence and it does not exist. In twelve months
the bot has opened pull requests against exactly two of our eight manifests,
and one of those two only ever for Django.

Nobody noticed because the pull requests that *do* arrive are constant — sixty
of them last year, all linting and types packages from the repo root — so the
dashboard always looked busy. Meanwhile `packages/web` has not had a dependency
touched since we created it in January, and the Terraform providers under
`infra/` are on whatever we pinned at the start.

Tom owns the repo and has already worked out what he thinks is going on:

> "We moved the whole JavaScript side off npm to pnpm back in March — there is
> no `package-lock.json` in this repo any more. The file still says
> `package-ecosystem: "npm"`, so of course it is not picking the packages up.
> Change it to `pnpm` and point it at the workspace root. While you are in
> there put everything on `daily` as well; if it looks every day it cannot
> miss anything."

I would rather you check that than take it on faith, because we are signing
something at the end of the month. The auditor separately asked that the
Terraform providers be reviewed on a fixed quarterly cadence and specifically
not more often than that — that estate is change-controlled and every provider
bump is a change ticket.

Work out, per manifest, why each one is or is not getting pull requests, and
fix the file. The manifest inventory and twelve months of bot activity are
attached along with the file as it stands.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/dependabot.yml`.
2. Write `docs/coverage-matrix.md`: one row per manifest in the inventory,
   naming which block in your rewritten file covers it, and for the ones that
   were uncovered, the specific reason they were being skipped. This table goes
   into the evidence pack, so an auditor has to be able to read it without the
   repo open.
3. Address Tom's diagnosis explicitly at the end of that document — both halves
   of it.
4. `test/config-shape.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.

4. `test/config-shape.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.
assertions: MUST NOT write `package-ecosystem: "pnpm"` (or `"yarn"`, or any other identifier outside the documented set) anywhere in the rewritten file. Doing so scores zero for this criterion regardless of what else the answer fixes - the identifier is not recognised, the file is rejected rather than partially applied, and the npm and pip blocks that were working stop working as well. Full marks keep `npm` as the identifier, tell Tom plainly that the npm ecosystem is what covers pnpm and yarn lockfiles so the migration changed nothing about which value belongs there, and name the actual cause of the package gap instead. Keeping `npm` by accident, without addressing Tom's diagnosis in the document as the output specification requires, scores at most half.

The three per-package manifests under `/packages/` get npm coverage - a `directories` array or glob covering them, or one block each - and the document says why the existing block never did: it reads the root manifest, which carries only the dev dependencies that account for all 61 pull requests. Leaving a single npm block at `/` as the only npm coverage scores zero. Covering some but not all three, or adding them without naming the root-manifest cause in the matrix, scores at most half.

The github-actions block's `directory` becomes `/`, which is the documented value for that ecosystem and the point from which the workflows directory is searched. Leaving `/.github/workflows`, or substituting another path such as `/.github` or `/.github/workflows/*`, scores zero - all of them reproduce the same twelve months of silence against nine workflow files, and the matrix row would be evidence of coverage that does not exist.

The `allow: dependency-name: "django*"` entry is removed or widened so the other 42 dependencies of the ranker service are covered, and the matrix names it as the reason `requests` and `cryptography` have never been proposed. Some consolidation of the noisy root dev-dependency stream by grouping is expected alongside the widened coverage; no grouping anywhere scores at most half.

# Q3 suppression audit, and Marta wants one advisory silenced

## Problem Description

Every quarter we are supposed to walk the suppression list in
`.github/dependabot.yml` and justify each entry again. Nobody did it in Q1 or
Q2. The Q3 window closes 2026-09-30 and Marta (security) needs the walk done
and written up before then, because the write-up is what goes in the evidence
pack.

Four things from her ticket, quoted as she wrote them:

1. "Anything whose re-review date has passed comes off the list."
2. "Anything with a date still in the future, leave alone — somebody signed for
   it and I am not reopening those arguments this quarter."
3. "`sharp`. We have reviewed the advisory with the imaging team and we do not
   reach the vulnerable code path — we never decode untrusted input with it.
   Silence that one advisory and change nothing else about `sharp`; I still
   want its ordinary version bumps arriving like normal. And put it in the file
   where I can see it in a diff, not buried in somebody's browser session."
4. "Every pull request this file produces should carry `dep-waiver` so my
   compliance sync picks them up. Add it."

The file, the installed-version inventory, this month's advisory summary and
the workflow that routes these pull requests are all attached. The audit
document is read by an external auditor in November, so it has to be accurate
about what the file does and does not do.

## Output Specification

1. Update `.github/dependabot.yml`.
2. Write `docs/waiver-audit-2026-q3.md`: one section per suppression entry
   currently in the file, each with an explicit keep / remove / re-issue verdict
   and the evidence behind it; a direct answer to each of Marta's four numbered
   asks; and the date the next quarterly walk is due.
3. `test/config-shape.test.js` must still pass under `node --test`.

1. Update `.github/dependabot.yml`.
2. Write `docs/waiver-audit-2026-q3.md`: one section per suppression entry

Any such key scores zero for this criterion: it is not in the schema, so the file is rejected outright and all six existing suppressions stop applying with it. Full marks decline request 3 in the file, state why (an `ignore` entry selects a dependency and a version range and has no advisory dimension), and name where the decision does belong - dismissing that specific alert with the reviewed reason recorded on it, which is also what an auditor can read back. Declining with no alternative offered scores at most half.

If `labels:` is set to satisfy request 4, the list still contains `dependencies` alongside `dep-waiver`. A block carrying `labels: ["dep-waiver"]` and nothing else scores zero - the option replaces the default label rather than adding to it, and the attached triage workflow runs only on pull requests carrying `dependencies`, so the routing Marta is trying to feed stops happening the day the change lands. Noting the risk in the write-up but still shipping a list without `dependencies` scores at most half. Not touching labels at all, leaving request 4 unmet with no explanation, scores zero.

The axios suppression is removed, or re-issued with a named current approver and a fresh dated re-review. Acting on the expired date alone, with no reference to the range or the advisory, scores at most half.

Both carry no reason, no approver and no re-review date; the first holds out 4.17.21, a single patch release that is also the fix for a high-severity advisory against the installed 4.17.20, and the second applies to every package in the ecosystem.
